manifest.sample:
# Starter project file. Rename the project before you publish it.
[project]
name = "example-app"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

files.body:
"""Starter package. Rename it before you publish it."""

__all__ = ["name"]


def name() -> str:
    """The package's name, so the starter has one thing its own test can check."""
    return "example-app"

"""Smoke test, so a new project's test command has something to run.

Written on `unittest` and reading the tree rather than importing it: this file
is written whether or not a runner was ticked, so it must pass under plain
`python -m unittest` with nothing installed. pytest collects a TestCase
unchanged. The assertion is a bare `assert` rather than `self.assertTrue`
because ruff's PT009 — which jig's own ruff config selects — refuses the
method form, and unittest runs either one.
"""

import unittest
from pathlib import Path


class SmokeTest(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_the_package_directory_is_here(self) -> None:
        package = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "src" / "example_app"
        assert package.is_dir()

"""Smoke test for the runner this project installed, so the package itself is
exercised and the coverage floor in pytest's addopts is reachable on a tree
with nothing in it. The import resolves through the `pythonpath` entry pytest's
own config carries. `python -m unittest` never sees this file: it discovers
`test*.py`, and pytest discovers `*_test.py` too, so the two runners each have
one file of their own and neither reads the other's.
"""

from example_app import name


def test_the_package_reports_its_name() -> None:
    assert name() == "example-app"

toolchain.why: Single fast linter that carries the pyflakes, bugbear, bandit, pytest-style, annotation, pygrep and tryceratops rule families, so most agent damage patterns have a named rule id here rather than needing a bespoke regex.
toolchain.configSample:
[tool.ruff]
line-length = 100
target-version = "py311"
src = ["src", "tests"]

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = [
  "E", "F", "W",
  "B", "S", "BLE", "PT", "PL", "TRY",
  "ANN", "PGH", "ERA", "DTZ", "T10", "T20", "RUF",
]
ignore = []

[tool.ruff.lint.per-file-ignores]
"tests/**/*.py" = ["S101"]

[tool.ruff.lint.flake8-pytest-style]
raises-require-match-for = ["*"]
toolchain.wiring: [tool.pdm.scripts] lint = "ruff check ."  (Poetry/pip projects: a Makefile target `lint: ; ruff check .`)

verify.expected: exit code 1, with one line per violation of the form `path/to/file.py:12:5: S110 `try`-`except`-`pass` detected, consider logging the exception` and a trailing `Found N errors.`

toolchain.why: Formatting drift is the noise that hides real diffs; --check fails CI on unformatted files without rewriting them, which no linter rule does.
toolchain.configSample:
[tool.ruff]
line-length = 100

[tool.ruff.format]
quote-style = "double"
indent-style = "space"
skip-magic-trailing-comma = false
docstring-code-format = true
toolchain.wiring: [tool.pdm.scripts] fmt = "ruff format ."  (CI runs the same binary with --check)

verify.expected: exit code 1, printing a unified diff per file followed by `N files would be reformatted`

toolchain.why: Only the type checker can tell that an imported module, attribute or call signature does not exist — the exact failure an agent produces when it invents an API, and one no regex or linter can see.
toolchain.configSample:
[tool.mypy]
python_version = "3.11"
files = ["src", "tests"]
strict = true
warn_unreachable = true
disallow_any_explicit = true
no_implicit_optional = true
enable_error_code = [
  "ignore-without-code",
  "possibly-undefined",
  "redundant-expr",
  "truthy-bool",
  "unused-awaitable",
]

disallow_untyped_defs = true
toolchain.wiring: [tool.pdm.scripts] typecheck = "mypy"  (config supplies `files`, so no path argument is needed)

toolchain.why: The only tool that proves the code still behaves; its exit codes also separate a failing suite (1) from a suite that never collected anything (5), which is how a 'done, tests pass' claim gets falsified.
toolchain.configSample:
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
minversion = "8.0"
testpaths = ["tests"]
pythonpath = ["src"]
addopts = "--strict-markers --strict-config --import-mode=importlib -ra --cov=src --cov-report=term-missing --cov-fail-under=85"
xfail_strict = true
filterwarnings = ["error"]
markers = [
  "slow: takes longer than a second",
]
toolchain.wiring: [tool.pdm.scripts] test = "pytest"  (addopts in pyproject.toml carries the strict flags, so a bare `pytest` is already strict)

verify.expected: exit code 1 with `FAILED tests/test_billing.py::test_invoice_total_applies_discount - AssertionError` and a `1 failed` summary; exit code 5 with `no tests ran` when the suite collected nothing

toolchain.why: Checks the resolved dependency set against the PyPI advisory and OSV databases — a class of breakage that lives entirely in the lockfile and that no linter, type checker or test touches.
toolchain.configSample:
# pip-audit has no config file of its own. With no -r it audits the interpreter
# that happens to be on PATH, which is a fact about the machine and not about
# this project; -r pins the input to this file, so the audit is reproducible and
# is about the code here. jig runs it that way in every lane.
#
# Empty on purpose: jig does not know what this project depends on, and a pin
# nobody chose is a dependency jig invented. Add your own here and the audit
# reads them.
toolchain.wiring: [tool.pdm.scripts] audit = "pip-audit --strict -r requirements.txt"  (uv/poetry projects: export first, e.g. `uv export --no-hashes -o requirements.txt`)

verify.expected: exit code 1 with `Found N known vulnerabilities in M package(s)` above a Name/Version/ID/Fix Versions table; exit code 0 and `No known vulnerabilities found` when clean

toolchain.why: Proves the package still installs and imports from a clean tree — catches a module an agent moved or a dependency it started importing without declaring, both of which pass every in-tree check because the working directory is on sys.path.

classes.title: Assertion softened into a tautology
agentModes: cannot work out why the assertion fails, so rewrites it as `assert x == x` or `assert True` and reports the test as passing
replaces a specific expected value with the actual value read back from the same call, making the assertion self-referential
reduces `assert result == 42` to `assert result is not None` when the arithmetic is wrong

fixtures.violation:
from decimal import Decimal

from billing import invoice_total


def test_invoice_total_applies_discount() -> None:
    total = invoice_total(subtotal=Decimal("100.00"), discount_pct=10)
    assert total == total
    assert True


def test_invoice_total_rejects_negative_discount() -> None:
    total = invoice_total(subtotal=Decimal("50.00"), discount_pct=0)
    assert total == total
fixtures.nearMiss:
from decimal import Decimal

from billing import invoice_total


def test_invoice_total_applies_discount() -> None:
    expected_total = Decimal("90.00")
    total = invoice_total(subtotal=Decimal("100.00"), discount_pct=10)
    assert total == expected_total


def test_invoice_total_is_idempotent() -> None:
    first = invoice_total(subtotal=Decimal("50.00"), discount_pct=0)
    second = invoice_total(subtotal=Decimal("50.00"), discount_pct=0)
    assert first == second

classes.gapNotes: Only catches the two most literal shapes. `assert result is not None`, `assert len(rows) >= 0` and `assert isinstance(x, object)` are equally hollow and match nothing here; ruff has no rule for `assert True` (B011 and PT015 cover only the always-false direction), so that half rests on the regex alone. A weakening that changes an expected constant to a laxer one (42 -> `> 0`) is invisible without diffing against the previous revision.

evidence.source: ruff rule page docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/comparison-with-itself/ confirms PLR0124 `comparison-with-itself` flags a name compared to itself.

classes.title: Test body replaced with an unconditional failure
agentModes: stubs a test it intends to write later as `assert False, "not implemented"` and never returns to it
converts a test it cannot make pass into a deliberate failure so the diff still 'has a test'
leaves `assert False` behind after using it to confirm a code path was reached

fixtures.violation:
import pytest

from config import parse_config


def test_parse_config_rejects_unknown_key() -> None:
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        parse_config({"unknown": 1})
    assert False


def test_parse_config_reads_timeout() -> None:
    assert False, "not implemented yet"
fixtures.nearMiss:
from config import parse_config


def test_parse_config_defaults_strict_off() -> None:
    config = parse_config({})
    assert config.strict is False


def test_parse_config_disables_cache() -> None:
    config = parse_config({"cache": False})
    assert config.cache is False
    assert not config.strict

classes.gapNotes: `pytest.fail("todo")` and `raise NotImplementedError` are the same abandonment and neither is matched — B011/PT015 will not fire on them either, and PT015 in fact steers authors toward `pytest.fail()`, so a codebase that takes the ruff fix moves the mistake out of detector range. `assert 0` also slips past the regex.

evidence.source: ruff rules index docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/ lists B011 `Do not \`assert False\`` and PT015 `Assertion always fails, replace with \`pytest.fail()\``; PT015 confirmed at docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/pytest-assert-always-false/.

classes.title: Test skipped or xfailed instead of fixed
agentModes: adds `@pytest.mark.skip(reason="flaky")` to the test blocking its change and moves on
calls `pytest.skip()` at the top of a test body so the failure disappears from the summary
marks a genuinely broken test `@pytest.mark.xfail` so a red suite reads green
classes.gapNotes: Skipping is legitimate — platform gates, optional extras, `@pytest.mark.skipif(sys.platform == 'win32')` — so this fires on the honest cases too and only earns its keep as a review prompt, not a block. `unittest.skip`, `unittest.expectedFailure` and a `pytest.ini` `-k` filter are all uncovered. `xfail_strict = true` catches only the narrow case of an xfail that has started passing; it says nothing about one that is genuinely still failing and has been parked for months.

evidence.source: pytest configuration reference: `xfail_strict` ini option makes an unexpectedly-passing xfail a failure; marker names confirmed in pytest's mark documentation.

classes.title: Test body emptied to pass
agentModes: deletes the failing assertions and leaves `pass` so the function still exists and the count of tests is unchanged
replaces the body with `...` while promising to restore it
keeps the test name and docstring but drops every call to the code under test
classes.gapNotes: No ruff or mypy rule exists for an empty test body, so this is regex-only. It sees only the two literal empty bodies: a test gutted down to `assert True`, to a lone `print()`, or to setup with every assertion removed still matches nothing. A test method inside a `TestFoo` class matches (the `def test_` prefix survives indentation), but a unittest method named `runTest` does not. Most importantly it cannot see a test that was deleted outright — for that, the `test-count-dropped` class in this edition counts `def test_` across an edit, and `--cov-fail-under` in pytest's addopts is the CI-side backstop. A body of docstring-then-`pass` is the common real shape and matches nothing, because the pattern needs `pass` immediately after the colon.

evidence.source: No documented linter rule covers empty test bodies; pattern derived from pytest's `test_` collection convention (python_functions default) documented in pytest's configuration reference.

classes.title: Early return short-circuits a test
agentModes: inserts `return` at the top of a failing test so it collects, runs and reports as passed while asserting nothing
wraps the assertions in a guard that is never true, leaving an early exit as the only reachable path
converts a test into a no-op after a refactor changed the fixture it depended on

fixtures.violation:
from auth import verify_token


def test_verify_token_rejects_expired() -> None:
    return
    assert verify_token("expired") is False


def test_verify_token_accepts_fresh() -> None:
    return None
    assert verify_token("fresh") is True

classes.gapNotes: Only catches a return as the very first statement. A return placed three lines in, after some harmless setup, matches nothing. mypy's `unreachable` code closes that gap but only when `--warn-unreachable` is on, which `--strict` explicitly does not enable — the config sample turns it on separately. A test that exits early via `if not FEATURE_ON: return` is reachable code and neither detector will complain.

evidence.source: mypy optional error code list (error_code_list2) documents `unreachable` — 'Statement is unreachable'; mypy command_line docs state --warn-unreachable is not enabled by --strict.

classes.title: Redefined test silently replaces the original
agentModes: appends a second `def test_x` at the end of the module instead of editing the existing one, so Python binds the last definition and the first test stops running
re-emits a whole test file after a partial read and duplicates functions it did not realise were already there
copies a test into a new module scope with the same name to 'fix' it, leaving both
classes.gapNotes: No regex detector: deciding that a name is redefined needs the whole module's binding table, and a pattern that merely counted `def test_` occurrences would flag every legitimate same-named method across sibling classes — exactly the near-miss above. F811 covers same-scope redefinition only; a test moved to a different module and left behind in the original is a duplicate no tool here reports.

evidence.source: ruff rules index docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/ lists F811 (pyflakes) 'Redefined while unused'.

classes.title: Exception caught and discarded
agentModes: cannot diagnose why a call raises, so wraps it in `try/except: pass` and calls the bug fixed
adds `except ...: continue` inside a loop so a batch job stops reporting the records it dropped
silences an exception surfaced by a new test rather than handling the condition the test describes

fixtures.nearMiss:
import contextlib
import json
import logging
from pathlib import Path

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


def load_records(paths: list[Path]) -> list[dict]:
    records: list[dict] = []
    for path in paths:
        try:
            records.append(json.loads(path.read_text()))
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            logger.warning("skipping unparseable file %s", path)
            continue
    with contextlib.suppress(KeyError):
        records.sort(key=lambda row: row["id"])
    return records

classes.gapNotes: Both the regex and S110/S112 look for `pass` or `continue` as the handler's first statement. A handler whose body is `return None`, `return []`, `self.errors += 1` or a bare `...` swallows just as thoroughly and is matched by nothing. `contextlib.suppress` — the idiomatic form the near-miss uses — is deliberately not flagged, which means an agent that reaches for it produces an undetectable version of the same mistake. Ruff's own S110 documentation frames this as 'consider logging', so teams that already log-and-continue will see the rule pass on handlers that still lose the error.

evidence.source: ruff rule page docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/try-except-pass/ confirms S110 `try-except-pass`; rules index confirms S112 '`try`-`except`-`continue` detected, consider logging'.

classes.title: Blind except catching everything
agentModes: widens `except ValueError` to `except Exception` when a second, unrelated error surfaces, rather than handling both
writes a bare `except:` around a block it does not understand, which also swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit
adds a catch-all around the whole request handler to make an intermittent failure stop appearing in logs
classes.gapNotes: Catching `Exception` at a process boundary — a task worker, a CLI entrypoint, a web framework's error middleware — is correct, and neither the regex nor BLE001 can tell that apart from a catch-all buried three functions deep. Aliased forms (`except builtins.Exception`, or `E = Exception; except E:`) evade the regex. `except BaseException*` exception-group syntax is not matched.

evidence.source: ruff rules index docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/ lists BLE001 'Do not catch blind exception' (flake8-blind-except) and E722 'Do not use bare `except`' (pycodestyle).

classes.title: Exception test that accepts any failure
agentModes: writes `pytest.raises(Exception)` so the test passes on an ImportError or a TypeError from its own broken setup, not the error under test
drops the `match=` argument when the message it guessed did not appear, leaving the assertion unable to distinguish two different failures
keeps `self.assertRaises(Exception, ...)` after narrowing was requested
classes.gapNotes: The regex only sees the literal `Exception`/`BaseException` spellings on one line; `pytest.raises(\n    Exception,\n)` split across lines matches neither pattern, and a project-wide alias for a broad base class defeats both. PT011 fires only for the exception types listed in `raises-require-match-for` — the config sample sets `["*"]`, which is stricter than ruff's default and will also flag narrow-but-unmatched raises, so expect noise before it settles.

evidence.source: ruff rule pages docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/assert-raises-exception/ (B017, flags assertRaises/pytest.raises on Exception or BaseException) and docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/pytest-raises-too-broad/ (PT011, requires `match` or `check`).

classes.title: Blanket type: ignore silences the checker
agentModes: appends `# type: ignore` to whatever line mypy complained about instead of fixing the type
adds `# mypy: ignore-errors` at the top of a module it could not get clean
uses a bare ignore that then also hides a second, unrelated error introduced later on the same line

fixtures.violation:
# mypy: ignore-errors
from external_sdk import Client


def fetch_user(client: Client, user_id: str) -> dict:
    raw = client.users.get(user_id)  # type: ignore
    return raw.to_dict()  # type: ignore
fixtures.nearMiss:
from external_sdk import Client


def fetch_user(client: Client, user_id: str) -> dict:
    raw = client.users.get(user_id)  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
    return raw.to_dict()  # type: ignore[no-any-return]

classes.gapNotes: This detector needs comments intact, so a comment that merely discusses an ignore — a review note, a changelog line — reads the same as a live suppression. A coded ignore is treated as clean, but `# type: ignore[misc]` is nearly as blanket as the bare form and passes every check here. Suppression by config — adding a module to `[[tool.mypy.overrides]]` with `ignore_errors = true` — is the same evasion moved into pyproject.toml and is not covered.

evidence.source: ruff rule page docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/blanket-type-suppression/ confirms PGH003; mypy optional error code list documents `ignore-without-code` — 'Type ignore comment without error code'.

classes.title: Type widened to Any to silence the checker
agentModes: changes a parameter annotation to `Any` when the real type is inconvenient to work out
returns `Any` from a function so every caller's checks dissolve downstream
annotates a dict payload as `dict[str, Any]` rather than defining the TypedDict the error was asking for
classes.gapNotes: Marked heuristic because `Any` at a genuine boundary — a `**kwargs` passthrough, a decorator wrapper, a deserialiser's input — is correct, and neither the regex nor ANN401 can see intent. The regex misses `cast(Any, x)`, `object` used as a stand-in, aliases such as `JSON = Any`, and implicit Any from an untyped third-party import (mypy's `no-any-unimported` covers that last one but is not wired here). ANN401 flags arguments only, so a widened return type rests on mypy's `explicit-any`, which requires --disallow-any-explicit and is not part of --strict.

evidence.source: ruff rule page docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/any-type/ confirms ANN401 `any-type`; mypy optional error code list documents `explicit-any` and command_line docs confirm --disallow-any-explicit is outside the --strict bundle.

classes.title: Blanket noqa disables the linter on a line
agentModes: appends `# noqa` to whatever line ruff flagged rather than resolving the finding
adds a bare noqa to a wildcard import, which then also hides every undefined-name error that follows
leaves stale noqa comments behind after the underlying violation was fixed, so future violations on that line are pre-suppressed

fixtures.violation:
import os  # noqa
import sys  # noqa
from legacy.util import *  # noqa


def env_or(name: str, default: str) -> str:
    return os.environ.get(name, default)  # noqa

classes.gapNotes: Runs with comments intact, so prose that merely mentions noqa gets flagged. A per-file suppression in `[tool.ruff.lint.per-file-ignores]`, or an entry added to the top-level `ignore` list, removes the same rule far more broadly and leaves no comment for either detector to see. RUF100 only catches a noqa that suppresses nothing today; a noqa carrying a real code that the author should have fixed is indistinguishable from a justified one.

evidence.source: ruff rule pages docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/blanket-lint-suppression/ (PGH004) and docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/unused-noqa/ (RUF100).

classes.title: Credential written into source
agentModes: pastes a key from the conversation or from a log into the module so the example it just wrote will run
sets a password as a function default to make a test pass without wiring up the fixture
inlines a token it found in another file rather than reading the environment variable that file used
classes.gapNotes: Name-driven and therefore heuristic in both directions. A secret stored under a neutral name (`CONFIG_VALUE`, `HEADER`, `X`) is invisible; so is one built by concatenation or base64-decoded at import. Conversely a placeholder such as `PASSWORD = "changeme"` in an example module trips it. The value has to be a single-quoted literal on one line, so a key assembled across a line continuation or held in a triple-quoted block is missed. It says nothing about a credential committed to a .env, a YAML fixture or a notebook, none of which are .py files. It also cannot revoke anything — a hit means the key is already in git history.

evidence.source: ruff rules index docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/ lists S105 'Possible hardcoded password assigned to', S106 '...assigned to argument', S107 '...assigned to function default' (flake8-bandit).

classes.title: Environment value hardcoded instead of read
agentModes: writes `http://localhost:8000` into the module because that is what worked in the session, instead of reading the configured base URL
hardcodes an absolute path from its own machine or container into a constant
compares against a bare status code or magic threshold rather than the named constant the codebase already defines

fixtures.nearMiss:
import os
from http import HTTPStatus
from pathlib import Path

import httpx

BASE_URL = os.environ["REPORTKIT_BASE_URL"]
CACHE_DIR = Path(os.environ.get("REPORTKIT_CACHE_DIR", "~/.cache/reportkit")).expanduser()


def fetch_report(report_id: str) -> dict:
    response = httpx.get(f"{BASE_URL}/reports/{report_id}", timeout=30)
    if response.status_code == HTTPStatus.TOO_MANY_REQUESTS:
        raise RuntimeError("rate limited")
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()

classes.gapNotes: Both regex shapes are literal: a loopback URL, and an absolute `/home`, `/Users`, `/root`, `/opt`, `/srv` or `/mnt` path, each written directly into a quoted string. An internal hostname that is not loopback (`api.staging.internal`), a bare IP, an S3 bucket, a tenant id, a port number on its own, and a path assembled by `os.path.join` or an f-string all match nothing, and neither shape can tell a value that belongs in source — a documented default, a protocol constant — from one that should have been read from the environment. PLR2004 covers the third agent mode only, and only where the magic value appears in a comparison rather than an assignment, which is the more common hardcoding; it is noisy by design, exempting 0, 1, empty string and `__main__` and nothing else.

evidence.source: ruff rule page docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/magic-value-comparison/ confirms PLR2004 `magic-value-comparison` and its exemptions.

classes.title: Invented import path, attribute or signature
agentModes: imports a helper that sounds right for the library but does not exist in the installed version
calls an attribute on a response or client object that it has confused with another library's API
references a module-level constant it believes it defined earlier in the session but never wrote

fixtures.violation:
from datetime import datetime

from httpx import AsyncClient, retry_policy


async def fetch_with_retry(url: str) -> str:
    policy = retry_policy(max_attempts=3)
    async with AsyncClient(retries=policy) as client:
        response = await client.get(url)
    stamp = datetime.utcnow().isoformat()
    return f"{stamp}:{response.text_body}:{BUILD_ID}"
fixtures.nearMiss:
from datetime import UTC, datetime

from httpx import AsyncClient, Limits

BUILD_ID = "dev"


async def fetch_with_retry(url: str) -> str:
    limits = Limits(max_connections=3)
    async with AsyncClient(limits=limits) as client:
        response = await client.get(url)
    stamp = datetime.now(UTC).isoformat()
    return f"{stamp}:{response.text}:{BUILD_ID}"

classes.gapNotes: No regex detector is possible — deciding a name does not exist requires resolving the installed distributions, which is exactly what mypy does and a pattern cannot. The coverage is only as good as the stubs: a dependency shipping no `py.typed` marker resolves to Any and every invented attribute on it passes silently (mypy reports `import-untyped` instead, and `--strict` treats that as an error only because `--disallow-untyped-calls` catches the call site). F821 sees undefined bare names but not undefined attributes. A signature invented for a function that does exist — wrong keyword argument, wrong arity — is reported under `call-arg`/`arg-type` rather than the codes listed here.

evidence.source: mypy error code documentation for `attr-defined` and `import-not-found`; ruff rules index lists F821 'Undefined name' (pyflakes).

classes.title: Debugger or print left in shipped code
agentModes: inserts `breakpoint()` or `pdb.set_trace()` while chasing a failure and does not remove it, hanging CI on stdin
leaves `print()` calls used to inspect intermediate values in library code that has a logger
keeps a debug import at the top of the module after the investigation ended

fixtures.violation:
import pdb

from pipeline import transform


def run(rows: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:
    out: list[dict] = []
    for row in rows:
        if row.get("status") == "error":
            breakpoint()
        pdb.set_trace()
        out.append(transform(row))
    print(out)
    return out

classes.gapNotes: T201 flags every `print`, which is wrong for CLI entrypoints and scripts — those need a per-file ignore or the class becomes noise the team learns to skip. The regex misses `import pdb; pdb.set_trace()` written through an alias, `debugpy.breakpoint()`, and `sys.breakpointhook` manipulation. Nothing here catches a debug side effect that is not a print or a debugger, such as a temporary file written to /tmp or an added `time.sleep`.

evidence.source: ruff rules index docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/ lists T100 'Trace found' (flake8-debugger) and T201 '`print` found' (flake8-print).

classes.title: Mutable default argument shared across calls
agentModes: writes `def f(items: list[str] = [])` when adding an optional collection parameter, producing state that leaks between calls
uses `{}` as a cache default and then mutates it, so the 'cache' silently becomes global
reproduces the pattern from an older file in the repository without noticing it is the bug being reported

fixtures.nearMiss:
def collect(item: str, bucket: list[str] | None = None) -> list[str]:
    bucket = [] if bucket is None else bucket
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket


def index(key: str, store: dict[str, int] | None = None) -> dict[str, int]:
    store = {} if store is None else store
    store[key] = store.get(key, 0) + 1
    return store

classes.gapNotes: The regex confines itself to a single-line parameter list and to three literal empty containers; a default spread over several lines, or a non-empty literal such as `= ["a"]`, or a mutable instance built by a call (`= Counter()`, `= datetime.now()`) all escape it. B006 covers those calls and multi-line signatures properly, so on a project with ruff wired the regex is a redundant fast path rather than the real detector. Neither sees a mutable class attribute, which produces the same shared-state bug one level up.

evidence.source: ruff rules index docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/ lists B006 'Do not use mutable data structures for argument defaults' (flake8-bugbear).

classes.title: Re-raise that discards the original cause
agentModes: wraps a caught error in a domain exception without `from exc`, so the traceback that would have identified the bug is gone from the logs
converts a library error into a generic RuntimeError with a message it invented, losing both type and cause
raises a fresh exception inside a handler to satisfy a test that asserts on the outer type
classes.gapNotes: Heuristic, and only fires when the raise is the handler's first statement and its argument list contains no nested parentheses — `raise ConfigError(f"bad {fmt(path)}")` defeats it, as does any handler that logs before raising. `raise X from None` is a deliberate suppression that reads as correct to both detectors even when the cause was worth keeping. B904 is the reliable half; the regex exists only so the class still reports on a repo where ruff is not yet running.

evidence.source: ruff rule page docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/raise-without-from-inside-except/ confirms B904 and its `__cause__` vs `__context__` rationale.

classes.title: Code commented out rather than removed
agentModes: comments out the failing block instead of deleting it, so a later session restores logic that was intentionally dropped
leaves the previous implementation commented above the new one as an undo buffer
comments out an assertion or a validation call to get a green run

fixtures.violation:

def report(rows: list[dict]) -> str:
    # def legacy_report(rows):
    #     return summarise(rows, mode="legacy")
    # import pandas as pd
    # assert rows, "no rows to summarise"
    return summarise(rows, mode="v2")

classes.gapNotes: Both detectors are heuristic and ruff's own documentation admits ERA001 is prone to false positives on comments that merely resemble code. The regex recognises six statement openers, so a commented-out expression, a commented call like `# validate(payload)`, or a block comment written with a docstring rather than `#` all pass. Because it needs comments intact it also matches the same text inside a docstring that is teaching the pattern. It cannot distinguish a deliberately preserved reference implementation from abandoned code.

evidence.source: ruff rule page docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/commented-out-code/ confirms ERA001 `commented-out-code` is stable and documents its false-positive tendency.

classes.title: Coverage pragma hides untested code
agentModes: adds `# pragma: no cover` to the branch it could not write a test for, so the coverage gate passes

Version-gated imports and `if TYPE_CHECKING:` blocks are legitimately excluded with the same pragma and will be flagged. The bigger evasion is invisible to this class entirely — adding patterns to `exclude_lines` in `[tool.coverage.report]`, or simply lowering `--cov-fail-under`, exempts code with no comment anywhere in the source.

evidence.source: coverage.py's default exclusion marker is the `# pragma: no cover` comment, with `# pragma: no branch` for partial-branch exclusion; no linter rule id exists for either.

classes.title: Shell invoked with interpolated input
agentModes: builds a command as an f-string and passes `shell=True` because the list form did not work first try
falls back to `os.system` when it cannot get argument quoting right
interpolates a filename or user-supplied identifier straight into a shell command

import subprocess


def archive(target: str) -> None:

Neither detector proves the interpolated value is attacker-controlled — a constant command with `shell=True` is flagged just as hard. classes.title: Untrusted data deserialized unsafely
agentModes: picks `pickle` to persist a session or cache because it round-trips arbitrary objects with no schema work

classes.gapNotes: `cPickle`, `dill`, `shelve`, `marshal` and `jsonpickle` are the same hazard under other names and match nothing. Neither detector can tell a pickle of the process's own trusted data from a pickle of a request body. S506 `unsafe-yaml-load` is the confirmed ruff code for the yaml half, but no detector here is wired to it, so that half stays regex-only.

evidence.source: ruff rule page docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/suspicious-pickle-usage/ confirms S301 and its arbitrary-code-execution rationale.

classes.title: Test collection quietly narrowed
agentModes: adds `collect_ignore_glob` to conftest.py so the failing integration module stops being collected, leaving a green run over a smaller suite
rewrites `items[:]` in a `pytest_collection_modifyitems` hook to filter out the tests it could not fix
narrows `testpaths` or appends `--ignore=` to addopts so the suite that 'passes' is not the suite that was asked for

fixtures.violation:
from __future__ import annotations

import pytest

collect_ignore_glob = ["test_integration_*.py"]


def pytest_collection_modifyitems(config: pytest.Config, items: list[pytest.Item]) -> None:
    items[:] = [item for item in items if "slow" not in item.keywords]

classes.gapNotes: Only looks at conftest.py, so the most common form of this — editing `testpaths` or `addopts` in pyproject.toml, or a `--ignore=` added to the CI command line — is entirely outside its reach and needs the CI step to pin the invocation instead. Deselecting via `items.remove(...)` in a loop, or via a `pytest_ignore_collect` hook, matches neither pattern. Marked heuristic because both shapes have legitimate uses: excluding a module that needs an optional dependency is normal, and reordering `items[:]` for deterministic run order is not narrowing at all. The real backstop is comparing the collected count across runs, which no detector here does.

evidence.source: pytest hook and conftest documentation for `collect_ignore` / `collect_ignore_glob` and the `pytest_collection_modifyitems` hook; no linter rule id exists for either.

classes.title: Dependency with a known advisory
agentModes: pins an older version because that is the API it remembers, reintroducing a fixed advisory
adds a dependency to solve a small problem without checking its advisory history
regenerates a lockfile from a stale constraint set and silently rolls a transitive dependency backwards
classes.gapNotes: There is no rule id to claim: pip-audit reports advisory identifiers (PYSEC-*, GHSA-*), not lint rules, so the detector names `--strict` — the flag that makes a collection failure fail the audit rather than pass quietly. The fixtures are illustrative only; the real signal lives in requirements.txt or the lockfile, which is not a .py file and which no check-driver pattern in this edition scans. A vulnerable version that has no advisory yet, and a vulnerability in vendored or system code, are both invisible. Results also shift under you as the advisory databases update, so a clean audit is a statement about today.

evidence.source: pip-audit project documentation: exits 1 when one or more known vulnerabilities are found, prints 'Found N known vulnerabilities in M package(s)'; `--strict` fails the audit if dependency collection fails.

classes.title: Fewer test cases after the edit than before it
agentModes: Deletes the failing test case and reports the suite green
Trims a parameterised case list down to the inputs that already pass
Removes the whole case rather than the assertion inside it, so no empty test body is left to find

classes.gapNotes: A removal is not in any file's content — the deleted case is absent from the file that is left, so a pathless check-driver run reports this class skipped and proves it only from the fixture pair, which carries the file before the edit and the file after it. The commit lane is the run that holds both versions: `--staged` counts the index against HEAD, a file deleted outright included, so a commit that shrinks the suite is a finding there. The earlier lane is an authored `edit-guard` on the same removal rule — a catalogue never carries a session guard, so that half is the owner's to author. It reads one edit at a time: an Edit payload carries the text it replaced, so a case deleted out of a test module is seen, and a Write payload carries none, so a whole-file rewrite that drops a test module is not. Author it to observe: one call cannot see the case being put back two calls later, and a deletion can be right — behaviour that genuinely went away takes its tests with it, which is a judgement no count can make.

evidence.source: No tool in the Python ecosystem gates on a drop in test count between two revisions; the runners report what they discovered, never what they stopped discovering. The judgement that a shrinking suite is a defect is jig's own.

classes.title: Stub left raising while the task is reported done
agentModes: Leaves `raise NotImplementedError` in a function whose signature and callers it already wrote
Marks the missing half with a TODO comment and reports the change complete
Returns None or an empty list from a function it did not write, so callers run and the suite passes vacuously
classes.gapNotes: Both tokens are also the correct code somewhere: `raise NotImplementedError` is the documented body of an abstract method, and a TODO comment is often a note about a later improvement over finished code — so this reports a guess about intent, not a fact, and needs a wave-off path. The near miss is the trap it does avoid: an @abstractmethod that declares its contract with a docstring rather than a raise, and a module constant named TODO_REVIEW_LIMIT that is code rather than a marker. The quietest form has no token at all — a body of `...`, `pass`, or a return of `None` written because the session did not know what to compute. Ruff's flake8-fixme rules (FIX001-FIX004) would name the comment half, but they are not in the select list jig installs, so no tool-rule detector is claimed for them.

evidence.source: NotImplementedError is documented in the Python built-in exceptions reference as the signal for an unimplemented abstract method; the comment markers are jig's own convention and carry no enabled rule id.

classes.title: sleep standing in for a real wait condition in a test
agentModes: Adds time.sleep to make an intermittently failing async test pass on the machine it is running on
Increases an existing sleep when the test fails again, rather than waiting on the condition
Sleeps because it does not know which awaiting primitive the project already has

fixtures.violation:
import asyncio
import time

from queueing import DispatchQueue


def test_drains_synchronously() -> None:
    queue = DispatchQueue()
    queue.submit("a")
    queue.submit("b")
    time.sleep(0.5)
    assert queue.pending_count() == 0


async def test_drains_asynchronously() -> None:
    queue = DispatchQueue()
    queue.submit("a")
    await asyncio.sleep(0.25)
    assert queue.pending_count() == 0

import asyncio

from queueing import DispatchQueue


def test_reports_sleep_budget() -> None:
    assert DispatchQueue().sleep_budget_millis() == 0


async def test_drains_asynchronously() -> None:
    queue = DispatchQueue()
    queue.submit("a")
    queue.submit("b")

No ruff rule bans it and none honestly could, so there is no tool-rule detector. It reads two spellings — a sleep imported directly (`from time import sleep`), a `trio.sleep`, an anyio sleep, or a busy-wait loop all carry neither. Scoped to the test paths, so the same sleep in a fixture module outside them is missed. The near miss holds the trap: `sleep_budget_millis` mentions sleeping without doing it, and `asyncio.wait_for` is a real condition wait on the same import.

evidence.source: time.sleep and asyncio.sleep are documented standard-library calls; the judgement that their use inside a test is a synchronisation smell is jig's policy, backed by no rule id — hence no tool-rule detector.
